En 1956, Kurt Gödel escribió una carta a: In 1956, Kurt Gödel wrote a letter to John von Neumann, who was by then very ill, asking him whether it could be decided in a number of steps proportional to $n$ or to $n^2$ whether a mathematical statement has a proof of length $n$. It was, in other words, the P versus NP question, fifteen years before Stephen Cook formulated it and made it famous. The letter was not known until the late nineteen-eighties. Leonid Levin, in the Soviet Union, reached the same results as Cook on his own at almost the same time.
En 1971, Stephen Cook demostró algo ines: In 1971, Stephen Cook proved something unexpected: there are problems in NP that are the hardest of all, in a precise sense. Any other problem of NP can be translated into them at polynomial cost. They are called NP-complete. The following year, Richard Karp showed that 21 classic problems were, and today thousands are known: generalised sudoku, colouring a map with three colours, the knapsack problem, the travelling salesman.
En [[av-computabilidad]] se vio que hay: In [[av-computabilidad]] we saw that there are problems no computer can solve, not with all the time in the world. But among the problems that can be solved there is another frontier, more practical and just as deep: the one separating those solved in seconds from those that would not finish before the end of the universe, even with a correct algorithm and the fastest computer there is. To measure it, powers, logarithms and the comparison of infinities from [[fn-limites|limits]] are enough.
Es $O(\\log n)$: multiplicar el tamaño p: It is $O(\log n)$: multiplying the size by a thousand only adds about ten comparisons.
Eso es lo que costaría mirar los element: That is what looking at the elements one by one would cost. Halving each time reduces the list far faster.
Eso sería si el coste creciera en propor: That would be so if the cost grew in proportion to $n$. Here the time grows like the cost of the algorithm.
Eso son los subconjuntos. Para ordenar,: Those are the subsets. For ordering, the first place has $n$ candidates, the second $n - 1$…: $n!$.
Factorizar y el logaritmo discreto se cr: Factoring and the discrete logarithm are believed to be hard; it is not proved, nor even that they are NP-complete. The internet rests on a reasonable conjecture.
Hasta $n = 40\\,000$: mil veces más: Up to $n = 40\,000$: a thousand times more
Hay una forma de bajar el coste que no c: There is a way of lowering the cost that does not change the algorithm: having another program rewrite yours as an equivalent, cheaper one. It is what a compiler does when optimising, and it is built in [[len-optimizar|folding constants and removing dead code]], where the improvement is also measured in two different numbers —how much space it takes and how many steps it does—, which is the distinction that here separates memory from time.
Intenta primero encontrar tú una combina: Try first to find a combination adding up to 100 yourself. How many attempts did it take you? Then see at which attempt the computer finds it trying in order.
La criptografía se apoya en problemas qu: Cryptography rests on problems believed to be hard, such as factoring enormous numbers or the [[av-cripto-curvas|discrete logarithm]]. Careful: those problems are not known to be NP-complete. They are in NP, they are believed not to be in P, but their hardness is not proved. The security of the internet rests on a very reasonable conjecture, not on a theorem.
Las empresas de transporte no calculan l: Transport companies do not compute the optimal route for delivering parcels, which is an NP-hard problem: they use heuristics that come within a few per cent of the optimum. Chip makers verify their designs with programs that solve the SAT problem, the first known NP-complete one, and which work astonishingly well on the cases that appear in practice, although in the worst case they are exponential.
Los costes polinómicos son manejables; l: Polynomial costs are manageable; exponential and factorial ones become impossible at modest sizes, however fast the computer.
Los informáticos llaman <strong>eficient: Computer scientists call algorithms whose cost is a polynomial in $n$ efficient: $n$, $n^2$, $n^{3}$. The problems that have such an algorithm form the class P. Sorting a list, finding the shortest path in a [[av-grafos|graph]] or telling whether a number is prime are in P.
Los problemas NP-completos son los más d: The NP-complete problems are the hardest in NP: if one were easy, they all would be. Nobody knows whether P = NP.
Los segundos dependen del ordenador. Se: Seconds depend on the computer. You count steps as a function of $n$, and look at how they grow: $O(n^2)$ today and in twenty years' time.
Mientras tanto, en la práctica se usan <: Meanwhile, in practice heuristics are used: methods that find good solutions, though not necessarily optimal ones, in a reasonable time.
Mil veces más rápido no significa mil ve: A thousand times faster does not mean a thousand times bigger. Each unit of $n$ doubles the work, so a thousand times only buys $\log_2 1000 \approx 10$ units.
Mil veces más velocidad con $2^n$ solo s: A thousand times more speed with $2^n$ only adds 10 to the reachable size. With $n^2$ it multiplies it by 31. The real improvement is always the algorithm.
NP significa que la solución se <em>comp: NP means the solution is checked quickly. All of P is in NP. The hard ones (if P ≠ NP) are the NP-complete ones, not any problem in NP.
P: problemas que se resuelven en tiempo: P: problems solved in polynomial time. NP: problems whose solutions are checked in polynomial time.
Para comparar algoritmos no se mide cuán: To compare algorithms you do not measure how many seconds they take, which depends on the computer, but how many basic steps they take as a function of the size $n$ of the problem: how many numbers have to be sorted, how many cities have to be visited. And the exact number is not of interest, but how it grows as $n$ becomes large.

The horizontal lines mark what a computer doing a thousand million steps a second gets through in a second, a day, a century and the age of the universe. Move n.
Pero hay muchísimos problemas para los q: But there are a great many problems for which nobody knows an efficient algorithm and which, even so, have a curious property: if someone gives you a solution, checking it is easy. Solving a giant sudoku is hard; checking a filled-in one, immediate. Finding a route passing through every city in under 1000 km is hard; checking one you are given only takes adding up. The problems whose solutions are checked in polynomial time form the class NP.
Probar todos los subconjuntos es exponen: Trying every subset is exponential; trying every ordering, worse still.

Everything that is solved quickly is checked quickly: solving it is enough. That is why P is contained in NP.

The question is whether they are equal: whether everything that is checked quickly can also be solved quickly. Almost everyone believes not, but nobody has proved it. It is one of the seven Millennium Problems, with a million-dollar prize since the year 2000.

Un ordenador mil veces más rápido no arr: A computer a thousand times faster does not fix an exponential algorithm. If $2^n$ steps take a day, the new computer in a day solves problems of size $n + 10$, because $2^{10} \approx 1000$. With a quadratic algorithm, the same jump in speed multiplies the reachable size by 31. The real improvement always comes from a better algorithm.
